after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration. 

$$
f(x)=\frac{6}{\sqrt[7]{x}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {0}^{+}
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt[7]{x}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{1}\frac{6}{\sqrt[7]{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}{\int }_{a}^{1}6{x}^{-1/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}7{x}^{6/7}{|}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}7\sqrt[7]{{x}^{6}}{|}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[7\cdot \sqrt[7]{{1}^{6}}-7\cdot \sqrt[7]{{a}^{6}}] \\  & =7(1)-7(0) \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The integrand is unbounded at x = -3, the upper endpoint. Replace that endpoint by b < -3 and take b → (-3)⁻, giving option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{-6}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}?$
after.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (-6,-3):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to (-3)^{-}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [-6,b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to (-3)^{-}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{-3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to (-3)^{-}}({\int }_{-6}^{b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\,\text{d}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫−6−3dxx2−9?

a
limb→(−3)−(∫−6b1x2−9dx)
b
limb→−∞(∫b−31x2−9dx)
c
limb→3−(∫−6b1x2−9dx)
d
limb→∞(∫−6b1x2−9dx)
e
limb→(−6)+(∫b−31x2−9dx)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the upper integration limit from any point that lies in the interval x∈(−6,−3):

f(x)=1x2−9→∞asx→(−3)−

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating f(x) over the interval x∈[−6,b] and taking the limit as b→(−3)−:

∫−6−31x2−9dx=limb→(−3)−(∫−6b1x2−9dx)

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option a: the singular upper endpoint −3 must be approached from the left while the lower endpoint remains −6. Option b instead extends the interval to −∞ and diverges.

content.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{-6}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}?$
content.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (-6,-3):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to (-3)^{-}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [-6,b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to (-3)^{-}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{-3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to (-3)^{-}}({\int }_{-6}^{b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\,\text{d}x)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{x(x+1)}?$
after.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *lower* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (0,2):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{x(x+1)}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {0}^{+}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [a,2]$ and taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{x(x+1)}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}({\int }_{a}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{x(x+1)}\,)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{-1}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{4-{x}^{2}}?$
after.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (-1,2):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{4-{x}^{2}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {2}^{-}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [-1,b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to {2}^{-}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{4-{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{b\to {2}^{-}}({\int }_{-1}^{b}\frac{\text{d}x}{4-{x}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{-1}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{4-{x}^{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (-1,2):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{4-{x}^{2}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to {2}^{-}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [-1,b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to {2}^{-}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{4-{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{b\to {2}^{-}}({\int }_{-1}^{b}\frac{\text{d}x}{4-{x}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the integral using a substitution. Let $u=3x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

We use the table below to change the limits:

| $x$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $22$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $64$ |

Carrying out the change of variable, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2/3}^{22}\frac{1}{(3x-2)^{1/3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{64}\frac{\text{d}u}{3{u}^{1/3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{64}\frac{\text{d}u}{{u}^{1/3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded at the *lower* limit of integration.

$$
f(u)=\frac{1}{{u}^{1/3}}\to \infty \,\text{ as }\,u\to {0}^{+}.
$$

Nonetheless, it is possible to calculate the integral by setting the *lower* bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to {0}^{+}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{64}\frac{\text{d}u}{{u}^{1/3}} & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{a}^{64}\frac{\text{d}u}{{u}^{1/3}} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{a}^{64}{u}^{-1/3}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\frac{3}{2}\,{u}^{2/3}|}_{a}^{64} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{2}{\sqrt[3]{{u}^{2}}|}_{a}^{64} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to {0}^{+}}[\frac{1}{2}\sqrt[3]{{64}^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt[3]{{a}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 16-0 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{2/3}^{22}\frac{1}{(3x-2)^{1/3}}\,\text{d}x=8.
$$
